segments.text: Stratigraphy studies layered (sedimentary) rocks and their sequence in time; paleontology studies the fossils preserved within them. Together they let geologists reconstruct the order and timing of Earth’s history, even where absolute dates are unavailable.

blocks.text: 1. Principles of stratigraphic correlation and relative age

blocks.text: 2. Unconformities and breaks in the rock record

segments.text: is a surface representing a significant gap in the rock record — either non-deposition or erosion removed the rock that would otherwise represent that time interval. Different types are recognised by the geometric relationship between the layers above and below: an
has tilted older layers beneath horizontal younger layers; a
has parallel layers above and below the gap; a
has sedimentary rock overlying older igneous or metamorphic rock. Recognising unconformities is essential because they represent “missing time” not directly recorded by any rock layer.

divides Earth’s 4.6-billion-year history into a hierarchy of named intervals (eons, eras, periods, epochs), based primarily on major changes observed in the fossil and rock record (particularly, historically, mass extinction events marking major boundaries, such as the one separating the Mesozoic and Cenozoic eras). Learning this scale’s broad structure — which era or period corresponds to which major fossil groups and geological events — provides an essential shared reference framework for the entire subject.

is any preserved evidence of past life, preserved through various processes (permineralization, where minerals fill original pore spaces; carbonization, leaving a carbon film; casts and molds; or, more rarely, unaltered preservation, such as insects in amber). Fossils are classified taxonomically (like living organisms) and are used for dating rock (biostratigraphy, point 5), reconstructing past environments (since many organisms have known specific environmental tolerances), and directly reconstructing evolutionary history.
uses the vertical distribution of fossils within rock sequences for correlation and relative dating. An ideal

has three characteristics: it was geographically widespread (found across many locations, allowing broad correlation), it existed for a relatively short geological time span (giving precise age resolution), and it is easily identified — an organism that evolved rapidly and dispersed widely (such as many extinct marine invertebrates) makes an especially useful index fossil for exactly these reasons.

blocks.text: 6. Broad stratigraphic framework and important examples

segments.text: At syllabus level, familiarity with the broad stratigraphic framework — recognising how relative dating principles, unconformities, the time scale, and biostratigraphy combine to interpret a real rock sequence or geological map — is more important than memorising every named regional formation; where specific regional (e.g., Pakistani) stratigraphic examples are required, referring to authoritative geological survey sources ensures current and locally accurate detail.

items.text: Relative dating principles (superposition, original horizontality, cross-cutting relationships) establish the order of geological events without requiring absolute ages.
Unconformities represent gaps in the rock record, classified by the geometric relationship between the layers above and below the missing interval.
The geological time scale organises Earth’s history primarily around major fossil-record changes, especially mass extinctions.
Fossils are preserved through several distinct processes and serve both dating (biostratigraphy) and paleoenvironmental reconstruction purposes.
An ideal index fossil is widespread, short-lived, and easily identified, making rapidly evolving, widely dispersed organisms especially valuable for precise correlation.
